query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of oxygen as an interstitial element to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can improve its oxygen resistance by forming ordered oxygen complexes, which can impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening, thus maintaining useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the cast state
generation.intervention: Addition of oxygen as an interstitial element
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 25-1000 °C, atmosphere: air, exposure time: up to 5 hours, loading: tensile and compressive
generation.mechanism: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes that impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxygen resistance and maintained mechanical performance
generation.boundary: Temperature: 1000 °C, atmosphere: air, exposure time: 5 hours, loading: tensile and compressive
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of oxygen addition required to achieve improved oxygen resistance is uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with untreated and oxygen-added equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples exposed to air at 800 °C for 5 hours
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-added sample shows no improvement in oxygen resistance or mechanical performance compared to the untreated sample, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
